newsitem.title: USA: Peru debt widens more as hostage siege continues.
newsitem.headline: Peru debt widens more as hostage siege continues.

text.p: Brady bonds followed U.S. Treasuries higher in relatively light trading, as all eyes remained focused on the hostage situation in Peru, which triggered a 55 basis points widening since the incident began, traders said.

As the hostage situation in Lima moved into its second day Peru (WI) Brady bonds came under more pressure, widening another 25 basis points on the heels of an initial 30 basis points widening on Wednesday, traders said.

Late Tuesday, Peruvian rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima and threatened to kill about 400 hostages, including high-ranking foreign diplomats, unless the government freed jailed comrades of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

"My sense is that the hostage takers have achieved their objective, which was to call attention to their movement...I think their mission has been achieved successfully according to terrorist objectives," Paul Leme, senior international economist at Goldman Sachs & Co.
"I think they'll try to offer a peaceful solution before Christmas so that they will maintain a positive read in the Peruvian public."
Analysts said, despite the widening in Peru debt, other Brady debt was unaffected by the events in Peru.
Venez Pars was up 3/4 at a 74-5/8 bid and Venez Flirbs gained an 5/8 to 87-5/8, traders said. Argentine Pars were up 1-1/8 at 62-1/2 while Argentine Frbs gained 7/8 to 86-1/8 bid.
Russia's dollar Vnesh were up 1/2 at 77-1/8 bid.

"I think it is very important to underscore that this is a completely unrelated event to Latin America," Leme said. "It's a sign for those analyzing Peru that the situation still poses some risk, but it seems to me that its still an isolated event...even within Peru."

Peru, which is seeking to restructure roughly $4.0 billion in principal and interest with its commercial bank creditors, caused some concerns that hostage situation could delay the Brady closing expected in the first quarter of 1997.
However, analysts said they do not expect the event to impact the timing of the closing of the Brady agreement.

"So far if you look at what's been happening in the market place I don't see broad evidence that it's affecting people's psychology," said Brian Barish, head of emerging market research at Lazard Freres.

"The real question is...is this just a one time thing that's happening in Peru, or does this portend to other large problems in other Latin American countries," Barish said. "I think on the surface you would have to say no."
Still, analysts agree Peru has come a long way with reform citing a remarkable stabilization program, courageous and bold structural reforms and very aggressive privatization program.

Yet, analyst still see challenges ahead because of the country's credit history, vulnerability in their economic base, particulary on the export side, problems with income distribution and poverty and potential political problems.

"Peru in my mind has always been expensive it's very much technically driven," said Goldman's Leme. "It's a very small issuer and I've always believed that 400 (basis points) was artificially rich compared with 575 (basis points) for Mexico." ((--Nancy Leinfuss, 212-859-1675))
